unit_overview.curriculum_focus: OCR GCSE (9–1) Ancient History J198/01 Section D: Alexander the Great, 356–323 BC.
unit_overview.disciplinary_threads: Discrete Recall (5m), Prescribed Source Inference (5m AO3), Prescribed Source Accuracy (5m AO3), Second-Order Explain (10m AO1+AO2), and Set-Sources Essay (20m: 10m AO3!).
unit_overview.non_specialist_summary: Follows Alexander chronologically from Pella (356 BC) to Babylon (323 BC) anchored 100% in OCR Appendix 5f Prescribed Set Sources (Plutarch, Arrian, Diodorus, Pompeii Mosaic, Alexander Sarcophagus, Astronomical Diary, and Lysimachus/Ptolemy coins).

lesson_1_1.curriculum_link: KT 1.1: Alexander’s youth; character, political and personal influence of Olympias; relationship with Philip.
lesson_1_1.hinge_question: Which parent left the deeper mark on young Alexander by 337 BC: Olympias or Philip II?
lesson_1_1.hinge_guidance: Top-band Q20* responses contrast Olympias’ Achilles/Zeus Ammon spiritual identity (Plutarch 2–3 + Lysimachus coin) against Philip’s practical mentorship at Bucephalas, Mieza, and Chaeronea (Plutarch 6–9).

misconceptions.misconception: Confusing the curved horn on Lysimachus’ silver tetradrachm with the Egyptian god Ptah.
misconceptions.correction: 2025 OCR Examiner Report highlight: the curved horn around Alexander’s ear is the ram’s horn of Zeus Ammon.

misconceptions.misconception: Dismissing Plutarch as "unreliable because he wasn’t born yet / wanted a bestseller".
misconceptions.correction: Explain that Plutarch wrote 2nd-century AD moral biography ("Lives, not Histories") using lost 4th-century BC court memoirs to highlight character virtues and flaws.

lesson_1_1.send_adaptation: Use the 140-word Exam-Cut extracts with Green Golden Quotes first, opening the Scene-Tabbed Full Set Text Modal one short tab at a time.
lesson_1_1.stretch_challenge: Compare Plutarch’s two rival traditions in Chapter 3.3–3.4 over whether Olympias encouraged or mocked Alexander’s claim to divine parentage.
lesson_1_1.safeguarding_impartiality: Contextualise ancient Macedonian royal polygamy and Greek gender stereotypes towards Epirote women historically and objectively.
